pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Describe how organisms depend on each other in different ecosystems.
- State the differences between an ecosystem and a habitat.
- Construct a food chain and a food web found in an ecosystem.

pages.title: What is an Ecosystem?
pages.body: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with each other and with the non living parts of their environment, such as soil, water, air and sunlight, all functioning together as a connected system. A pond, a forest, a grassland and a coral reef are all examples of ecosystems, each with its own particular mix of organisms and physical conditions.

The exact physical location of one specific organism
questions.e: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with each other and with the non living parts of their environment, such as soil, water, air and sunlight, all functioning together as a connected system.

pages.title: Ecosystem Versus Habitat
pages.body: A habitat is the specific physical place where a particular organism lives, such as a termite mound, a riverbank or a tree hollow, while an ecosystem is the much broader community of interacting organisms and their environment within which many different habitats exist side by side. For example, a single forest ecosystem contains many different habitats within it, the leaf litter on the forest floor, the bark of a particular tree, and the canopy high above, each supporting different organisms, yet all connected as part of the same larger ecosystem.

pages.title: Living and Non living Components of an Ecosystem
pages.body: Biotic components, meaning the living organisms in an ecosystem, and abiotic components, meaning the non living physical and chemical factors, together make up the full composition of any ecosystem. Biotic components include producers, such as green plants, consumers, such as herbivores, carnivores and omnivores, and decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi. Abiotic components include sunlight, temperature, water, soil type and the gases present in the air, all of which influence which organisms can survive in a particular ecosystem and how well they thrive there.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How Organisms Depend on Each Other

pages.title: How Organisms Depend on Each Other
pages.body:
Feeding relationships, competition for resources, and mutually beneficial partnerships are three broad ways organisms within an ecosystem depend on one another. Feeding relationships link producers, consumers and decomposers together, since energy and nutrients pass from one organism to another as they eat and are eaten. Competition occurs when different organisms rely on the same limited resource, such as sunlight, water, or a particular type of food, and this competition can shape which species thrive in a given area. Mutually beneficial partnerships, such as the relationship between leguminous plants and nitrogen fixing bacteria studied earlier in this strand, show how some organisms depend on each other so closely that neither could thrive as well alone.

[[pic:A labelled diagram of a pond ecosystem, showing biotic components such as algae, fish, frogs and water birds, alongside abiotic components such as sunlight, water and dissolved oxygen, with simple arrows showing at least one feeding relationship, for example algae being eaten by small fish, which are eaten by a larger fish or bird.]]

Notice how this single ecosystem contains many interacting biotic and abiotic components at once, and how removing or disturbing even one part, such as reducing the amount of sunlight reaching the algae, could affect every other organism that ultimately depends on that algae for food.

pages.title: Food Chains
pages.body: A food chain is a single, straight line pathway showing how energy passes from one organism to the next, beginning with a producer and continuing through one or more levels of consumers. For example, in a grassland ecosystem, grass, a producer, may be eaten by a grasshopper, a primary consumer, which may in turn be eaten by a lizard, a secondary consumer, forming the simple food chain grass, grasshopper, lizard.

questions.q: Which of the following is an abiotic component of an ecosystem?
questions.e: Abiotic components include sunlight, temperature, water, soil type and the gases present in the air, all of which influence which organisms can survive in a particular ecosystem and how well they thrive there.

o: A network of many interconnected feeding pathways
A single, straight line pathway of feeding relationships
The total number of species in an area
questions.e: A food chain is a single, straight line pathway showing how energy passes from one organism to the next, beginning with a producer and continuing through one or more levels of consumers.

questions.e: Competition occurs when different organisms rely on the same limited resource, such as sunlight, water, or a particular type of food, and this competition can shape which species thrive in a given area.

pages.title: Food Webs
pages.body: A food web is a more realistic, interconnected network showing how many different food chains overlap within the same ecosystem, since most organisms eat, and are eaten by, more than one other species. Constructing a food web for a chosen ecosystem, by identifying several producers and consumers and drawing arrows to show every feeding relationship between them, gives a much fuller picture of how energy moves through that ecosystem than a single food chain alone.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Because organisms in an ecosystem are so interconnected through feeding relationships, competition and partnerships, a change affecting even one species can ripple outward to affect many others, an idea that becomes especially important in the next lesson, which examines how various interferences can disturb the balance of an entire ecosystem.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Predict and justify predictions on how interferences such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, hunting, farming, mining, galamsey, pollution, pesticides and bush burning will affect the balance in an ecosystem.

pages.title: What is Ecosystem Balance?
pages.body: Ecosystem balance refers to a stable, sustainable state in which the populations of organisms within an ecosystem, and the physical conditions around them, remain within a range that allows the whole system to keep functioning healthily over time. Building on Lesson 5, which described how organisms in an ecosystem depend on each other, this lesson looks at how various natural and human related interferences can disturb that balance, sometimes severely and sometimes only temporarily.

questions.q: Ecosystem balance refers to
o: A completely unchanging ecosystem with zero variation ever
A stable state that allows an ecosystem to keep functioning healthily
The total destruction of an ecosystem
The total number of humans living nearby
questions.e: Ecosystem balance refers to a stable, sustainable state in which the populations of organisms within an ecosystem, and the physical conditions around them, remain within a range that allows the whole system to keep functioning healthily over time.

pages.title: Earthquakes
pages.body: An earthquake is a sudden, violent shaking of the ground caused by movement deep within the Earth. A severe earthquake can destroy plant cover, disrupt water sources by altering underground channels, and directly kill or displace animals, sometimes changing the physical shape of a habitat so significantly that surviving organisms can no longer find shelter or food in their usual locations, forcing them to migrate or perish.

pages.title: Volcanic Eruptions
pages.body: A volcanic eruption releases hot lava, ash and gases that can destroy vegetation and kill animals over a wide area very quickly. Volcanic ash falling over a larger surrounding region can block sunlight needed for photosynthesis and contaminate water sources, while gases released during an eruption can alter air quality, sometimes affecting ecosystems far beyond the immediate eruption site. Over the longer term, however, volcanic ash can also enrich soil with minerals, meaning some ecosystems eventually recover with improved fertility.

questions.q: An earthquake can disturb an ecosystem mainly by
o: Destroying plant cover and disrupting habitats
questions.e: A severe earthquake can destroy plant cover, disrupt water sources by altering underground channels, and directly kill or displace animals, sometimes changing the physical shape of a habitat so significantly that surviving organisms can no longer find shelter…

o: Guaranteeing permanent ecosystem destruction with no recovery
questions.e: Volcanic ash falling over a larger surrounding region can block sunlight needed for photosynthesis and contaminate water sources, while gases released during an eruption can alter air quality, sometimes affecting ecosystems far beyond the immediate eruption…

pages.title: Hunting
pages.body: Hunting, when carried out excessively or without proper management, can reduce the population of a hunted species faster than it can naturally reproduce, sometimes to the point of local extinction. Since many organisms are connected through feeding relationships, studied in Lesson 5, removing too many individuals of one species can affect predators that depend on it for food, or allow prey species that it used to control to increase excessively, disturbing the balance of the wider ecosystem.

pages.title: Farming
pages.body: Farming, when it involves clearing natural vegetation to create fields, can reduce the variety of habitats available in an area, replacing a diverse natural ecosystem with a much simpler one dominated by a single crop species. Farming can also introduce new abiotic conditions, such as altered soil structure from ploughing, or changed water availability from irrigation, both of which can favour some organisms while disadvantaging others that depended on the original, undisturbed ecosystem.

questions.q: Excessive hunting can disturb ecosystem balance mainly by
o: Reducing a species faster than it can reproduce
Removing the need for any food chain
questions.e: Hunting, when carried out excessively or without proper management, can reduce the population of a hunted species faster than it can naturally reproduce, sometimes to the point of local extinction.

questions.q: Farming can disturb ecosystem balance mainly by
o: Increasing habitat diversity in every case
Reducing habitat diversity by replacing it with a single crop
Removing the need for soil entirely
questions.e: Farming, when it involves clearing natural vegetation to create fields, can reduce the variety of habitats available in an area, replacing a diverse natural ecosystem with a much simpler one dominated by a single crop species.

pages.title: Mining and Galamsey
pages.body: Mining, including illegal, poorly regulated small scale mining commonly known in Ghana as galamsey, can severely disturb ecosystem balance by removing vegetation, digging large pits that destroy soil structure, and releasing harmful chemicals, such as mercury used in some gold extraction methods, into nearby rivers and streams. Water bodies affected by mining activity often become heavily polluted and unable to support fish and other aquatic organisms, with effects that can persist for many years even after mining activity stops.

pages.title: Pollution
pages.body: Pollution introduces harmful substances into the air, water or soil of an ecosystem, often as a by product of industrial, agricultural or household activity. Polluted water can kill fish and other aquatic life directly, or accumulate in organisms over time and cause harm further along the food chain, including to humans who eat affected fish. Air pollution can damage the leaves of plants and affect the health of animals that breathe it, while soil pollution can reduce the fertility of land and harm the organisms living within it.

questions.q: Galamsey (illegal small scale mining) commonly pollutes rivers mainly through
o: Chemicals such as mercury used in extraction
Excess oxygen released into the water
questions.e: Mining, including illegal, poorly regulated small scale mining commonly known in Ghana as galamsey, can severely disturb ecosystem balance by removing vegetation, digging large pits that destroy soil structure, and releasing harmful chemicals, such as mercury…

questions.q: Pollution can affect an ecosystem by
o: Harming organisms in air, water or soil
Having no effect on any organism
questions.e: Air pollution can damage the leaves of plants and affect the health of animals that breathe it, while soil pollution can reduce the fertility of land and harm the organisms living within it.

pages.title: Pesticides
pages.body: Pesticides are chemicals used to kill unwanted insects, weeds or fungi on farms, and while they can protect crops from damage, they can also harm non target organisms if used carelessly, including beneficial insects such as bees that pollinate crops, and organisms further along the food chain that consume affected plants or insects. Pesticide residues can also wash into nearby water bodies, affecting aquatic ecosystems well beyond the farm where they were originally applied.

pages.title: Bush Burning
pages.body:
Bush burning, whether deliberate, for land clearing, or accidental, destroys plant cover rapidly, killing many smaller organisms directly and removing food and shelter for surviving animals. Repeated bush burning over several seasons can also degrade soil quality, as studied in relation to the nitrogen cycle earlier in this strand, making it harder for the original vegetation to recover fully, sometimes allowing hardier, less diverse plant species to dominate the area instead.

[[pic:A before and after comparison illustration of a river ecosystem, the before panel showing clear water, healthy vegetation along the banks, and visible fish, and the after panel showing the same river affected by galamsey mining, with muddy, discoloured water, destroyed vegetation, and no visible fish, with a short caption summarising the changes.]]

Notice how a single interference, in this case mining activity, can visibly transform an entire ecosystem, damaging water quality, vegetation and animal populations all at once, illustrating why predicting the effects of such interferences is such an important skill.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Predicting and Justifying the Effects of Interferences

pages.title: Predicting and Justifying the Effects of Interferences
pages.body: Considering which biotic and abiotic components are directly affected, tracing likely knock on effects through feeding relationships, and considering whether the ecosystem is likely to recover, and how quickly, are three useful steps for predicting and justifying how a particular interference will affect ecosystem balance. For example, predicting the effects of galamsey on a river ecosystem might reasonably conclude that fish populations will decline sharply due to water pollution, that animals depending on fish for food will be forced to find food elsewhere or decline themselves, and that recovery is likely to be slow, since removed vegetation and contaminated water can take years to return to their original condition even after mining stops.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

While natural interferences such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions are largely unavoidable, most of the human related interferences studied in this lesson, hunting, farming, mining, pollution, pesticide use and bush burning, can be managed more responsibly through regulation, community awareness and more sustainable practices, reducing the extent to which they disturb ecosystem balance while still allowing people to meet their needs.

The price of land in the area only
